name: Gateway of Last Resort
brief:
R1 sits at the edge of the school network. Everything it does not have a specific route for should go to R2. Rather than writing a route for every network in the world, write one default route and read what it does to the routing table.

R2 already knows the way back.
watchFor: A default route is 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 — a prefix that matches everything with a prefix length of zero, so it loses to every other route in the table. That is exactly what you want.

tasks.text: On R1, run show ip route and confirm the gateway of last resort is not set.
Add a default route on R1 pointing at 10.0.0.2.
Prove PC1 can now reach PC2.
Now also add the specific route to 192.168.20.0/24 via 10.0.0.2, so both routes exist at once.
tasks.hint: Both can live in the table. The router picks the longest prefix match, which is the /24, not the /0.

tasks.text: Confirm connectivity still works with both routes present.

extension: Point the default route at 10.0.0.99 instead — an address with nothing on it. Does the ping fail loudly or quietly? Explain to a teammate why a wrong default route is harder to spot than a missing one.
debrief: A default route is a promise that somebody else knows the way. That makes it powerful at the edge of a network and dangerous in the middle of one, because a packet sent to the wrong default does not bounce — it simply goes somewhere it should not, quietly.
